subject: Distributed and Cloud Computing

questions.text: State and explain Brewer's CAP Theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance). Explain why a distributed system can guarantee at most two of the three properties under network partitions. Compare Strong Consistency, Sequential Consistency, and Eventual Consistency.

Explain the architecture of Remote Procedure Call (RPC) and Java RMI. Describe the roles of Client Stub, Server Stub, Parameter Marshalling, and Dispatcher. Compare At-Least-Once, At-Most-Once, and Exactly-Once delivery semantics.

questions.chapter: Cloud Computing Architecture and Service Models
questions.text: Compare Cloud Service Models: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS) with shared responsibility architectural diagrams. Compare Public, Private, Hybrid, and Community cloud deployment models.

Explain Cloud Virtualization techniques: Full Virtualization, Paravirtualization, and Hardware-Assisted Virtualization. Compare Hypervisor-based Virtual Machines (VMs) with OS-level Containerization (Docker) in terms of isolation, resource overhead, startup latency, and density.
What is a Web Service? Why is RESTful web service more popular than SOAP-based web service in today's distributed application development? Explain with real-world examples.
How is Enterprise Application Integration different from legacy middleware systems? Explain the benefits of N-tier distributed architecture over monolithic architecture in software development.
Describe the mechanism of database connection pooling in high-traffic enterprise applications. What are the major considerations for creating and sizing an efficient connection pool?
What is Inversion of Control (IoC)? Explain the different techniques how Dependency Injection (DI) is implemented in distributed application frameworks.
Explain Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) concepts and design principles. Compare Service-Oriented Architecture with Microservices architecture in distributed cloud deployments.
Explain Enterprise Java Beans (EJB) architecture with its importance. List out the differences between Session Beans (Stateless, Stateful, Singleton) and Message-Driven Beans.
Explain Clock Synchronization in distributed systems: Lamport's Logical Clocks and Vector Clocks. Prove that if event $a$ happened-before event $b$ ($a \to b$), then $C(a) < C(b)$.
Explain Election Algorithms in distributed systems: (a) The Bully Algorithm, and (b) The Ring Election Algorithm. Trace message exchanges and state updates when the current coordinator node crashes.
Explain the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) atomic transaction protocol in distributed systems. Describe the Voting Phase, Commit Phase, and coordinator recovery mechanisms under failure.

Explain the architecture of the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS): NameNode, DataNodes, Secondary NameNode, chunk block replication ($128\text{ MB}$), and rack awareness. Explain the MapReduce distributed computational model with WordCount dataflow.

questions.chapter: Cloud Computing Architecture and Service Models
questions.text: Write short notes on: (a) Edge Computing versus Cloud Computing, (b) Facade Design Pattern in enterprise tiers, (c) Web 3.0 and data decentralization.

Explain Elasticity and Auto-Scaling in cloud infrastructure. Differentiate between Horizontal Scaling (Scale-Out/Scale-In) and Vertical Scaling (Scale-Up/Scale-Down). Describe live virtual machine migration.

Explain Lamport's Logical Clocks and Vector Clocks. Prove the happens-before relationship and causal ordering of events in distributed systems. Trace vector timestamps for a three-process communication scenario.
questions.solutionOutline: Lamport scalar clocks assign monotonically increasing counters L(e) to events: if a -> b, then L(a) < L(b), but converse does not hold (cannot detect concurrent events). Vector clocks assign vector V of size N: Vi[j] represents process Pi knowledge of Pj clock. If V(a) < V(b), then a causally precedes b, enabling precise detection of concurrency.

questions.text: Explain Distributed Mutual Exclusion algorithms: Centralized algorithm, Ricart-Agrawala algorithm, and Maekawa's voting algorithm. Compare message complexity and synchronization delay.
questions.solutionOutline: Centralized: 3 messages per CS entry/exit (single point of failure). Ricart-Agrawala: broadcasts timestamped request to all N-1 nodes; enters CS only after receiving OK from all; requires 2(N-1) messages. Maekawa: divides N nodes into voting subsets of size K approx sqrt(N); process enters CS upon receiving grants from its quorum; requires 3*sqrt(N) messages.

questions.text: Explain Coordinator Election Algorithms in distributed systems: Bully Algorithm and Ring Algorithm. Trace coordinator election when the highest priority process crashes.
questions.solutionOutline: Bully algorithm: any process detecting coordinator failure sends ELECTION message to all processes with higher IDs. If no answer, process declares itself coordinator and sends COORDINATOR message to all lower IDs; if higher ID answers, higher ID takes over. Ring algorithm: processes organized in logical ring; election token circulates collecting active process IDs; highest ID elected.

questions.text: Explain the Byzantine Generals Problem. Prove why consensus cannot be reached among $m$ faulty (arbitrary/malicious) generals unless the total number of generals is at least $3m + 1$ under oral messaging.
questions.solutionOutline: Byzantine fault models components that can fail arbitrarily and send conflicting, contradictory information. For 3 generals (1 traitor, m=1), loyal general cannot distinguish whether commander or other lieutenant is traitor (requires N >= 3m+1 = 4). Solved using oral message algorithms OM(m) with m rounds of message forwarding or cryptographic digital signatures.

questions.text: Explain the Raft Consensus Algorithm. Describe Leader Election, Log Replication, Term numbers, and Safety guarantees compared with Multi-Paxos.
questions.solutionOutline: Raft decomposes consensus into understandable sub-problems. Nodes in states: Follower, Candidate, Leader. Leader election uses randomized election timers and RequestVote RPCs. Log replication: Leader receives client commands, appends to log, broadcasts AppendEntries RPCs to followers, committing entry upon majority ACK. Safety: candidate must possess all committed entries to win election.

questions.text: Explain Two-Phase Commit (2PC) and Three-Phase Commit (3PC) protocols for distributed atomic transactions. Why is 2PC a blocking protocol upon coordinator crash?
questions.solutionOutline: 2PC guarantees all distributed participants either commit or abort. Phase 1 (Prepare): coordinator asks can-commit; participants respond yes/no. Phase 2 (Commit): coordinator sends global-commit if all yes, else global-abort. Blocking: if coordinator crashes during Phase 2 after participants voted yes, participants remain blocked holding locks indefinitely. 3PC inserts Pre-Commit state to avoid blocking under fail-stop assumptions.

questions.text: Describe Hypervisor Virtualization: Type-1 (Bare-Metal) vs Type-2 (Hosted). Explain hardware-assisted virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) and full virtualization vs paravirtualization.
questions.solutionOutline: Type-1 hypervisors (ESXi, Xen, KVM) run directly on host hardware; high performance, enterprise cloud servers. Type-2 hypervisors (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) run on top of host OS. Full virtualization runs unmodified guest OS using binary translation or VT-x hardware root/non-root modes. Paravirtualization modifies guest OS kernel with hypercalls (Xen) for lower virtualization overhead.

questions.text: Explain Containerization and OS-level virtualization. Compare Docker containers with Virtual Machines (VMs) in terms of startup latency, kernel sharing, resource overhead, and isolation.
questions.solutionOutline: Containers isolate user-space processes sharing host OS kernel using Linux kernel namespaces (pid, net, mnt, ipc) and cgroups (CPU, memory resource limits). Comparison: Containers share host kernel (millisecond startup, megabyte footprints, high density); VMs emulate hardware with separate guest OS kernel (minute startup, gigabyte footprint, hardware-level isolation).

questions.text: Explain Container Orchestration with Kubernetes (K8s). Describe Control Plane components (API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controller Manager) and Worker Node components (Kubelet, Kube-proxy, Container Runtime, Pods).
questions.solutionOutline: Automates deployment, scaling, and operations of containerized applications. Control Plane: kube-apiserver (REST API gateway), etcd (distributed key-value store for cluster state), kube-scheduler (assigns pods to nodes), kube-controller-manager (maintains desired state). Worker Node: kubelet (node agent enforcing pod specs), kube-proxy (network packet forwarding/load balancing), Pod (atomic unit of co-located containers).

questions.text: Explain the MapReduce programming paradigm. Formulate the Map and Reduce functions for word count and inverted index generation with execution flow across Mappers and Reducers.
questions.solutionOutline: Processes large datasets in parallel across clusters. Map: (k1, v1) -> list(k2, v2). Shuffling & Sorting: partitions intermediate keys and groups values by key: (k2, list(v2)). Reduce: (k2, list(v2)) -> list(k3, v3). Word count: Map outputs (word, 1); Reduce sums counts for each word. Inverted index: Map outputs (word, docID); Reduce aggregates unique docIDs for search index.

questions.text: Describe the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) architecture: NameNode, DataNodes, Block Replication (default 3x), Heartbeat signals, and Secondary NameNode checkpointing.
questions.solutionOutline: Master/slave distributed file system for large sequential data streaming. Files split into large blocks (128MB). NameNode stores metadata and block mapping in RAM and EditLog/FsImage. DataNodes store physical blocks on local disks. Default 3x replication places 2 copies on same rack, 1 on remote rack for rack-fault tolerance. Secondary NameNode merges EditLog into FsImage periodically to prevent log bloat.

questions.chapter: Cloud Computing Architecture and Service Models
questions.text: What is Serverless Computing (Function-as-a-Service - FaaS)? Explain cold start latency, event-driven triggers, stateless execution, and autoscaling compared with containerized microservices.
questions.solutionOutline: Cloud execution model where cloud provider dynamically manages machine resource allocation (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions). Developer deploys individual functions executing on event triggers (HTTP request, database write). Cold start: delay when spinning up new container instance upon idle invocation. Stateless design enables instantaneous auto-scaling from 0 to thousands of concurrent requests.

questions.text: Explain Distributed File Systems: Network File System (NFS) vs Andrew File System (AFS). Compare caching strategies, file state management, and consistency semantics.
questions.solutionOutline: NFS (v3): stateless server, block-level caching at client with periodic validation checks; simple crash recovery but high network traffic and weak consistency. AFS: stateful server, whole-file caching on client local disk, callback mechanism (server notifies client when cached file modified); highly scalable for campus networks with session-level consistency (changes visible upon file close).

questions.text: Explain Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and Microservices. Compare RESTful APIs and gRPC (Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2 multiplexing) for inter-service RPC communication in distributed cloud platforms.
questions.solutionOutline: Microservices decompose application into loosely coupled, independently deployable services organized around business domains. REST uses JSON over HTTP/1.1; human-readable, universal browser support, but high payload overhead and textual serialization cost. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2; strongly typed contracts, multiplexed bidirectional streaming, high performance for backend inter-service calls.
